source_title: Foreign gadget bans: all the news about the FCC’s clampdown on Chinese tech
source_excerpt:
What do drones , routers , and Roombas have in common? The US government wants to keep Chinese ones from entering the country. They’re the first consumer gadgets that are facing de facto import bans because of the US government’s xenophobic stance — and they might not be the last.
Originally, the US government was just worried about US networks. It’s been distrustful of Chinese telecom equipment providers Huawei and ZTE for well over a decade , eventually requiring telecom providers to “rip and replace” their gear . (Many telecoms have still failed to do so .) It established an “Entity List” for companies whose gear should be banned from import, marketing, and sale.
But under the second Trump administration, that list has been weaponized against entire home consumer gadget categories too — starting in December 2025 when Trump and Brendan Carr’s FCC banned all future foreign drones unless their companies obtained a waiver.
Next was a ban on all future foreign routers, all future foreign robots and power inverters , and within the robot ban, all future foreign robovacs. In each case, the government claims it’s because those gadgets fundamentally pose an unacceptable threat to US national security. But in each case, the US has provided zero public evidence of a threat, has done nothing about existing drones and routers and robots that might pose such a threat, and hasn’t given us any reason to trust that its waivers have anything to do with security .
Besides, there are rarely any US companies to fill the gaps left by foreign ones. Consumer gadgets are largely made overseas, including practically all routers and practically all drones — just like how your Apple, Dell, and HP laptops are not made in the US.
In this StoryStream, we’re following the latest on the foreign gadget bans.

His stated reasoning makes some sense, but it also omits important context: today’s test labs are concentrated in China because that’s where gadgets are made. Oct 21 Sean Hollister Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us A TP-Link Wi-Fi 8 router. Image: TP-Link TP-Link, one of the world’s leading manufacturers of consumer Wi-Fi routers, is in a precarious position in the US. The company just launched its first Wi-Fi 8 routers , but can’t bring them here because of President Donald Trump’s foreign router ban . Even though competitors Netgear and Asus make their routers in Asia, they’ve mysteriously obtained blanket waivers for all their new gear ; perhaps because of alleged ties to China , TP-Link hasn’t managed to get such a waiver yet. But TP-Link is willing to do something those companies weren’t — to invest nearly $1 billion to make routers in the United States , creating “hundreds of high-paying research and development, manufacturing, and construction jobs for American workers over the next four years,” according to a letter TP-Link sent to the FCC. Oct 15 Sean Hollister Unlike Netgear and Asus, TP-Link says it’s prepared to spend $1 billion to make Wi-Fi routers in the US. “TP-Link would begin assembling these Wi-Fi 8 devices in the United States by next year,” it claims in a letter to the FCC — if the FCC will exempt its routers from the foreign router ban . Oct 10 Sean Hollister The FCC plans to ban all Chinese labs from testing US gadgets by 2029. The FCC has been cracking down on some Chinese test labs that improperly helped authorize gadgets for import into the US — now, it wants to get rid of Chinese labs altogether starting December 2028, only authorizing labs if they have a reciprocal economic relationship with the US. It’ll vote on October 29th; you can read the whole argument here . The FCC says China has only 25 percent of the world’s test labs but tests 82 percent of the equipment. Oct 6 Sean Hollister The FCC has decertified two more Chinese test labs. The US has been finding ways to stem the tide of imported Chinese gadgets , including decertifying “bad labs” that are “apparently controlled by China.” It’s now pulled credentials from two more: SLG-CPC Test Laboratory , and Shenzhen STS Test Services , “for willfully providing incorrect or false equipment test results in connection with applications for equipment authorization.” It’s also planning to do the same to Shenzhen CTB Testing.

Sep 30 Sean Hollister Asus won’t say how it escaped the US router ban Photo by The Verge This spring, the United States banned all future foreign-made consumer routers — effectively all future routers — unless their makers could 1) convince the US government that they weren’t a national security threat, and 2) submit “a detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.” As of September 9th, Asus now has an exemption from the ban, just in time to bring its first early Wi-Fi 8 routers here. Aug 21 Sean Hollister HoverAir’s transforming modular drone has already been halted in the US The HoverAir Versa. Image: HoverAir I am so sorry, fellow US gadget fans: the FCC’s drone ban appears to have struck again. The HoverAir Versa — a baby steadycam with snap-on propeller wings that transform it into a drone — has already stopped taking US orders just three days after its Indiegogo debut , and may be forced to abandon shipping plans in the US. HoverAir is now telling backers it’s only shipping its camera to the US, not the piece that turns it into a drone, “due to a few remaining logistics updates with the Flight Kit.” But those “logistics” may actually be a euphemism for “we’ve been banned by the federal government.” The FCC’s database no longer has an entry for the HoverAir Versa at all, suggesting that its authorization grant has been pulled. Image: HoverAir HoverAir drones always have intriguing gimmicks. This one folds flat to fit in your pocket. This one can land on water. Another can charge inside its carrying case. Jul 31 Jennifer Pattison Tuohy The ban on robot vacuums won’t make them safer, only worse All future robot vacuums manufactured outside the USA (i.e., all of them) have been banned by the FCC. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge No other gadget knows as much about your home as a robot vacuum . They map your space, learn your routines, and many now carry a camera and microphone into every room in your house. As AI gives them a better understanding of what they see, the privacy and security risks these autonomous robots pose are only growing. That’s why greater scrutiny makes sense, but the ban on foreign-made mobile robots issued by the Federal Communications Commission earlier this week — implemented to address “unacceptable risks to the national security of the United States or the safety and security of United States persons” — doesn’t actually judge products by how secure they are, just where they’re built . It effectively means no new robot vacuums from major companies can enter the US market unless they are built here. And spoiler alert: none are. Read Article >
